event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness in All 55 counties Ahead of Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of strong low pressure tracked up the eastern seaboard downstream of a digging positive to neutrally tilted trough. Deep moisture through the dendritic growth zone and strong forcing resulted in widespread significant snowfall accumulation greater than 6 across the entire county warning area with amounts generally falling between 10-18. Localized amounts under narrow frontogenetically-forced bands reached up to 22 inches. An intruding mid-level warm nose reduced snow amounts slightly in northern West Virginia and resulted in a period of some mixing of snow with freezing rain and sleet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snow accumulation generally around 6 inches was reported by the Public across the county.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness in All 55 counties Ahead of Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong 1033 mb high pressure nosing ridging in from the west allowed for efficient radiational cooling and minimum wind chill values dropping below -15F, and as cold as -27F, in the higher elevations of Eastern Tucker County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County-wide minimum wind chill values ranged from -13 to -20 degrees early on the 20th with the coldest value of -27 degrees recorded by a mesonet site 5 miles east of Canaan Heights.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness in All 55 counties Ahead of Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong 1042 mb high pressure centered just to the northwest of the area provided plenty of subsidence and optimal conditions for cold temperatures overnight with wind chills dropping into the negative teens. A typical cold spot in Eastern Tucker County recorded a -25F reading from a mesonet site 5 miles east of Canaan Heights.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill values ranged from -10 to -20 across most of the county with the exception being a -25 degree reading from a mesonet site 5 miles east of Canaan Heights.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 4.0 inches of snow, up to 2.7 inches of sleet, and up to 0.20 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness in All 55 counties Ahead of Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties as Major Winter Storm Approaches
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. Other nights, Cold Weather Advisories were in effect. For the Allegheny Mountains, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. Further east, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties as Major Winter Storm Approaches
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties as Major Winter Storm Approaches
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 4.8 inches of snow, up to 2.5 inches of sleet, and up to a trace of freezing rain. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties as Major Winter Storm Approaches
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of strong low pressure tracked up the eastern seaboard downstream of a digging positive to neutrally tilted trough. Deep moisture through the dendritic growth zone and strong forcing resulted in widespread significant snowfall accumulation greater than 6 across the entire county warning area with amounts generally falling between 10-18. Localized amounts under narrow frontogenetically-forced bands reached up to 22 inches. An intruding mid-level warm nose reduced snow amounts slightly in northern West Virginia and resulted in a period of some mixing of snow with freezing rain and sleet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snow accumulation generally around 6 inches was reported by the Public across the county.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties as Major Winter Storm Approaches
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong 1042 mb high pressure centered just to the northwest of the area provided plenty of subsidence and optimal conditions for cold temperatures overnight with wind chills dropping into the negative teens. A typical cold spot in Eastern Tucker County recorded a -25F reading from a mesonet site 5 miles east of Canaan Heights.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill values ranged from -10 to -20 across most of the county with the exception being a -25 degree reading from a mesonet site 5 miles east of Canaan Heights.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties as Major Winter Storm Approaches
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 4.0 inches of snow, up to 2.7 inches of sleet, and up to 0.20 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties as Major Winter Storm Approaches
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night.||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. Gauges recorded flooding on the West Fork River, Buckhannon River, Sand Run, Tygart Valley River, South Fork Hughes River, and Middle Island Creek. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. Minor flooding was also recorded by the Weston, Enterprise, and Macfarlan gauges.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over 300 homes were without power in and south of Powellton due to tree damage.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties Due to Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front, trailing upper level low pressure, drove into West Virginia throughout the day on July 18th. The presence of a warm, moist, and unstable environment ahead of the front, coupled with mid-level energy, facilitated the development of showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. The heavy downpours that accompanied the first round of activity in the morning set forth flash flooding across the northern half of the state, with creeks spilling out of their banks onto local roadways. By later in the afternoon, daytime heating helped to support strong to severe thunderstorms, with damaging wind gusts causing downed trees and power lines across the north-central lowlands. While more convection threatened to the west, the environment over West Virginia became overworked by the evening rush hour, causing encroaching storms to quickly weaken before crossing into the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down, blocking the road at the intersection of WV-47 and Fink Creek Road outside of Linn.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties Due to Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent frontal system interacted with a very unstable airmass over a broad area from the Midwest to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Clusters of thunderstorms produced scattered damaging wind gusts in the afternoon and evening. A cluster of supercells spawned five tornadoes over the mountainous region of eastern West Virginia and western Virginia in the mid afternoon to mid evening hours. This event was notable for where the tornadoes occurred. For example, two tornadoes occurred in Pendleton County, WV--the first tornadoes in the county since 1998; one tracked for over 12 miles across multiple ridgelines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado descended on the 5100 block of Back Creek Road. Here, there was roof and siding damage to the house and outbuildings. On this farm property and to the east through unpopulated forest, thousands of trees were downed (80 to 90 percent at one point just east of property), many of which were hardwoods 1-2 feet thick snapped at the trunk.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties Due to Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms quickly developed in the late afternoon hours along and ahead of an approaching cold front. High dew points in the low 70s with upper 70s air temperatures were supportive of 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear, plenty for storm organization. Storms congealed and moved southeast through the area in broken line segments producing swaths of wind damage and a couple embedded tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree reported down on Hardin Run Road.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties Due to Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front, trailing upper level low pressure, drove into West Virginia throughout the day on July 18th. The presence of a warm, moist, and unstable environment ahead of the front, coupled with mid-level energy, facilitated the development of showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. The heavy downpours that accompanied the first round of activity in the morning set forth flash flooding across the northern half of the state, with creeks spilling out of their banks onto local roadways. By later in the afternoon, daytime heating helped to support strong to severe thunderstorms, with damaging wind gusts causing downed trees and power lines across the north-central lowlands. While more convection threatened to the west, the environment over West Virginia became overworked by the evening rush hour, causing encroaching storms to quickly weaken before crossing into the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage along Langley Road resulted in local power outages.

Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties Due to Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front, trailing upper level low pressure, drove into West Virginia throughout the day on July 18th. The presence of a warm, moist, and unstable environment ahead of the front, coupled with mid-level energy, facilitated the development of showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. The heavy downpours that accompanied the first round of activity in the morning set forth flash flooding across the northern half of the state, with creeks spilling out of their banks onto local roadways. By later in the afternoon, daytime heating helped to support strong to severe thunderstorms, with damaging wind gusts causing downed trees and power lines across the north-central lowlands. While more convection threatened to the west, the environment over West Virginia became overworked by the evening rush hour, causing encroaching storms to quickly weaken before crossing into the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed at the intersection of Right Freemans Creek Road and Bear Fork near Churchville.

None of the farm buildings sustained significant damage, nor did the house on the property. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough descended into the northeast quadrant of the United States while a surface low ambled east across Ontario and Quebec. The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night.||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. Gauges recorded flooding on the West Fork River, Buckhannon River, Sand Run, Tygart Valley River, South Fork Hughes River, and Middle Island Creek. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. Minor flooding was also recorded by the Weston, Enterprise, and Macfarlan gauges.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed on Tilden Road south of Beckley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough descended into the northeast quadrant of the United States while a surface low ambled east across Ontario and Quebec. The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night.||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. Gauges recorded flooding on the West Fork River, Buckhannon River, Sand Run, Tygart Valley River, South Fork Hughes River, and Middle Island Creek. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. Minor flooding was also recorded by the Weston, Enterprise, and Macfarlan gauges.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hickory Flat Run exceeded its banks near Walnut Drive. Significant flooding impacted homes on Morgan Addition Road, trapped residents in homes on Old Elkins Road, and stranded vehicles on Pinnell Street. A swift water rescue occurred on Little Sand Run and Bailey Ridge Road. Up to three feet of water flooded Stony Run Road near Route 20 South Road.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Emergency for All 55 Counties Due to Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along and out ahead of an approaching cold front in two rounds. One in southeastern Ohio through northern West Virginia in the afternoon hours and then another in northwestern Pennsylvania in the early evening. The environment was potent for severe weather with 2000-3000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear of 40-50 knots, notable curvature to hodographs with 100-200 m2/s2 of 0-1 km storm relative helicity, and precipitable water values above the 95th percentile. These parameters supported an all hazards day with supercells and line segments producing damaging wind, tornadoes, small hail, and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on Barker Run Road.

The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night.||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. Gauges recorded flooding on the West Fork River, Buckhannon River, Sand Run, Tygart Valley River, South Fork Hughes River, and Middle Island Creek. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. Minor flooding was also recorded by the Weston, Enterprise, and Macfarlan gauges.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple downed trees and power lines were observed on Hunters Fork Road.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness for All 55 Counties Ahead of Severe Weather Systems
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front, trailing upper level low pressure, drove into West Virginia throughout the day on July 18th. The presence of a warm, moist, and unstable environment ahead of the front, coupled with mid-level energy, facilitated the development of showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. The heavy downpours that accompanied the first round of activity in the morning set forth flash flooding across the northern half of the state, with creeks spilling out of their banks onto local roadways. By later in the afternoon, daytime heating helped to support strong to severe thunderstorms, with damaging wind gusts causing downed trees and power lines across the north-central lowlands. While more convection threatened to the west, the environment over West Virginia became overworked by the evening rush hour, causing encroaching storms to quickly weaken before crossing into the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down, blocking the road at the intersection of WV-47 and Fink Creek Road outside of Linn.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness for All 55 Counties Ahead of Severe Weather Systems
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent frontal system interacted with a very unstable airmass over a broad area from the Midwest to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Clusters of thunderstorms produced scattered damaging wind gusts in the afternoon and evening. A cluster of supercells spawned five tornadoes over the mountainous region of eastern West Virginia and western Virginia in the mid afternoon to mid evening hours. This event was notable for where the tornadoes occurred. For example, two tornadoes occurred in Pendleton County, WV--the first tornadoes in the county since 1998; one tracked for over 12 miles across multiple ridgelines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado descended on the 5100 block of Back Creek Road. Here, there was roof and siding damage to the house and outbuildings. On this farm property and to the east through unpopulated forest, thousands of trees were downed (80 to 90 percent at one point just east of property), many of which were hardwoods 1-2 feet thick snapped at the trunk.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness for All 55 Counties Ahead of Severe Weather Systems
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms quickly developed in the late afternoon hours along and ahead of an approaching cold front. High dew points in the low 70s with upper 70s air temperatures were supportive of 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear, plenty for storm organization. Storms congealed and moved southeast through the area in broken line segments producing swaths of wind damage and a couple embedded tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree reported down on Hardin Run Road.

The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night.||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. Gauges recorded flooding on the West Fork River, Buckhannon River, Sand Run, Tygart Valley River, South Fork Hughes River, and Middle Island Creek. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. Minor flooding was also recorded by the Weston, Enterprise, and Macfarlan gauges.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and power lines were downed onto Grass Run Road.

About 30 to 50 percent of trees were damaged on property in the 400 block of Thunder Road, with trees mostly uprooted in a convergent pattern. The tornado tracked east-northeast. None of the farm buildings sustained significant damage, nor did the house on the property. The tornado crossed the road and tracked up a hillside across the street with continued tree damage before dissipating after about|two minutes.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness for All 55 Counties Ahead of Severe Weather Systems
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front, trailing upper level low pressure, drove into West Virginia throughout the day on July 18th. The presence of a warm, moist, and unstable environment ahead of the front, coupled with mid-level energy, facilitated the development of showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. The heavy downpours that accompanied the first round of activity in the morning set forth flash flooding across the northern half of the state, with creeks spilling out of their banks onto local roadways. By later in the afternoon, daytime heating helped to support strong to severe thunderstorms, with damaging wind gusts causing downed trees and power lines across the north-central lowlands. While more convection threatened to the west, the environment over West Virginia became overworked by the evening rush hour, causing encroaching storms to quickly weaken before crossing into the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down onto the roadway along County Road 24 at Mt Zion Road.

The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night.||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. Gauges recorded flooding on the West Fork River, Buckhannon River, Sand Run, Tygart Valley River, South Fork Hughes River, and Middle Island Creek. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. Minor flooding was also recorded by the Weston, Enterprise, and Macfarlan gauges.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed on James River Road.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness for All 55 Counties Ahead of Severe Weather Systems
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along and out ahead of an approaching cold front in two rounds. One in southeastern Ohio through northern West Virginia in the afternoon hours and then another in northwestern Pennsylvania in the early evening. The environment was potent for severe weather with 2000-3000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear of 40-50 knots, notable curvature to hodographs with 100-200 m2/s2 of 0-1 km storm relative helicity, and precipitable water values above the 95th percentile. These parameters supported an all hazards day with supercells and line segments producing damaging wind, tornadoes, small hail, and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on Barker Run Road.

event_description: Governor Morrisey Declares State of Preparedness for All 55 Counties Ahead of Severe Weather Systems
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front, trailing upper level low pressure, drove into West Virginia throughout the day on July 18th. The presence of a warm, moist, and unstable environment ahead of the front, coupled with mid-level energy, facilitated the development of showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. The heavy downpours that accompanied the first round of activity in the morning set forth flash flooding across the northern half of the state, with creeks spilling out of their banks onto local roadways. By later in the afternoon, daytime heating helped to support strong to severe thunderstorms, with damaging wind gusts causing downed trees and power lines across the north-central lowlands. While more convection threatened to the west, the environment over West Virginia became overworked by the evening rush hour, causing encroaching storms to quickly weaken before crossing into the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Berry Run spilled out of its banks and flooded the entrance ramp from US-50 to I-77 south.
